The central loss in discarding the adjudicatory model in favor of 
notice and comment rulemaking was * * * the focused and defined 
record which all the procedures used in adjudication were intended 
to produce. This record served as the basis for decision both at the 
agency level and on review. There is at present in informal 
rulemaking no parallel requirement that the record certified to the 
court be the fi?uit of special procedures designed to produce it.
Is the Gurfein/McGowan description of the “record” in informal rulemaking an 
adequate response to this criticism?
There is httle doubt that Pedersen’s critique influenced judicial 
interpretation of the procedural requirements of section 553 of the APA. For 
exflTriple, in Solite Corp. v. EPA, 952 F.2d 473, 484 (D.C. Cir. 1991), a challenge 
to EPA hazardous waste regulations, the court declared:
The APA requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include 
“either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of 
the subjects and issues involved,” and that the agency “give 
interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rulemaking 
through submission of written data, views, or arguments.” Integral 
to the notice requirement is the agency’s duty “to identify and make 
available technical studies and data that it has employed in reaching 
its conclusions.”
Judge Gurfein’s insistence that an agency engaged in rulemaking make 
sure that the critical studies and other material that it rehes upon be made 
pubhc in time for affected persons to digest and respond to the agency’s 
“evidence” has impheations for its handling of comments that include 
supporting or rebuttal information. If such information is genuinely new and 
not simply cumulative, the agency may be obhgated to publish a notice of its 
submission and allow additional time for the fifing of responsive comments. 
Compare Air Transport Ass^n v. FAA, 169 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 1999) (failure to 
allow comments on critical new information denied petitioners fair notice), 
with Building Industry Assn of Superior California v. Norton, 247 F.3d 1241 
(D.C. Cir. 2001) (study received after comment period need not be disclosed if 
it addressed issues that were fully ventilated during the comment period).

The Obligations to Solicit and Bespond to Comments. In Nova Scotia 
Food Products, Judge Gurfein was critical not only of what he took to be the 
agency’s insufficient transparency as to its thinking, but also with regard to its 
failure to respond to issues raised by those comments the FDA did receive. It

the duty to “give reasoned responses to all significant comments in a
